title: What EMDR actually feels like
author: Shayla Martinez-O'Brien, LPC
excerpt: People often arrive expecting something dramatic. It is quieter and more ordinary than that, and the ordinariness is part of why it works.
heroAlt: Low sunlight through a stand of tall pines, falling across a quiet path.
body: The most common question I get in a first session is some version of: what is this going to feel like? Usually underneath it is a more specific worry — that EMDR means being made to relive the worst thing that ever happened to you, in detail, out loud, in front of a stranger.
It isn't that. And I'd rather say so plainly than let anyone spend a week dreading an appointment.
## The first sessions aren't processing at all

We spend the first session or two on history and groundwork. What you're carrying, what sets it off, what already helps on a bad day. Nothing gets opened before there's something steady to come back to.

Then we build what are called resourcing skills — practical ways to bring your body back down when it spikes. People sometimes treat this part as the boring preamble before the real work. It isn't. It's what makes the rest of it safe, and a fair number of people notice things easing before we touch a single memory.

You hold a piece of the memory in mind — an image, a physical sensation, a belief about yourself that came out of it — while following a repeating left-right cue. Usually that's my fingers moving across your field of vision, or tapping, or alternating tones through headphones.

You are not asked to narrate. You don't have to tell me what came up unless you want to. Sets are short, thirty seconds or so, and we pause between each one. You can stop at any point, for any reason, without explaining.

Most people say it feels a bit strange for the first minute and then unremarkable. Some feel tired afterward, the way you do after a long conversation. Some feel lighter almost immediately. Both are normal.

Over a series of sessions the memory tends to lose its charge. That's the clearest way I can put it. It doesn't disappear and it isn't rewritten — you'll still know what happened. What changes is that it stops arriving as though it's happening now.
People describe it as the memory moving from the front of the room to the back. Still there. No longer setting the terms.
We close every session deliberately, so you leave settled rather than opened up. That's not a courtesy, it's part of the protocol.

You don't need to have decided anything to have a first conversation. A consultation is fifteen minutes, free, and mostly me listening. If EMDR isn't the right fit for what you're carrying, I'll say so — that's a normal outcome, not a failure.
